title: Apify MCP tool cost: 10 live Actor definitions plus the tokens in their results
author: Philip Kirkbride
summary: I enabled ten of our Apify Actors on the hosted MCP server and counted 27,797 reference tokens in their tool definitions. Then I pulled the first three rows from a real run of each Actor. The biggest response, from our rental scraper, took 7,434 tokens . Asking for the same rows with just the fields I needed cut that to 298 . For a Claude or Cursor workflow, those are two separate levers. The tool list determines what definitions are available to the client. The dataset request determines the size of the result it can pass to the model. Ten live tools, three rows each I ran each Actor and used get-dataset-items on its default dataset with limit=3 . Each call returned three rows at offset zero. The tool definitions came from one tools/list response with the ten named Actors enabled on https://mcp.apify.com . I used the current server and runs on November 18, 2026 UTC. Actor under automatic/ Run input in brief Tokens per tool definition Tokens per three-row MCP result companies-house-scraper Search for Tesco companies 2,049 1,259 crypto-fear-greed Three days with market data 2,063 1,656 crypto-funding-rates BTC, ETH and SOL on Hyperliquid 2,080 1,231 wikipedia-pageview-spikes English Wikipedia, November 15 2,434 2,081 youtube-search-scraper Search for SQLite tutorials 2,533 1,395 google-maps-places-scraper Coffee shops in London, Ontario 2,724 3,664 google-news-scraper Search for SQLite news 2,775 2,510 trustpilot-reviews-scraper Chewy reviews 3,279 3,348 treasury-yield-curve Daily nominal and real yields, November 9–13 3,526 6,483 inmuebles24-mx-scraper Apartment rentals in Polanco 4,341 7,434 The 27,797 figure counts the ten definitions together as a JSON array. The complete array, including the server's four shared run and storage tools, was 31,598 tokens. The Treasury response was larger than the reviews response in this sample. Its rows include rate and change fields across maturities, so a small row limit can still produce a large result. Same dataset, fewer fields On the Polanco run, I kept the dataset, offset, and limit the same, and requested fields="price,currency,totalAreaM2,bedrooms" . The full MCP result went from 7,434 to 298 tokens, a 96% reduction . The first listing still had null for total area and bedrooms. Projecting fields keeps the source values, including missing ones. If you're calculating price per m², ask for the area and currency as well as the price. Inmuebles24 Actor Field filter Rows Full MCP result tokens All fields 3 7,434 price,currency,totalAreaM2,bedrooms 3 298 Apply this in Claude or Cursor Use a workflow-specific Apify connection when you know the Actor you need. For example, https://mcp.apify.com?tools=automatic/inmuebles24-mx-scraper selects the rental Actor alongside shared run and storage tools. A smaller tool list reduces the definition payload available to a client that loads tools eagerly. For an exploratory session, broader discovery can still be useful. After the run, ask for a preview with the fields the task needs. For example, “Read three items from the run's default dataset with the fields price, currency, totalAreaM2, and bedrooms. Keep nulls. Show the unit and source currency.” If you need a calculation over the whole dataset, run it in code and pass the summary to the model. These are payload measurements with a common tokenizer. Your model's tokenization, tool loading, caching and handling of MCP results determine how much of that payload reaches the model and what it costs. The full result here includes both MCP text content and structured content, which carry overlapping data. Read the provider's actual usage for a billable token count. Count it yourself Capture the JSON-RPC response to tools/list and one response to tools/call for get-dataset-items . For an SSE response, use the JSON from the matching data: line. Save those JSON-RPC messages as tool-list.json and dataset-call.json . The response body to count is the inner result object, with the JSON-RPC envelope removed. The list and each definition are counted separately. import json from pathlib import Path import tiktoken encoding = tiktoken . get_encoding ( "cl100k_base" ) def count ( value ) : wire = json . dumps ( value , ensure_ascii = False , sort_keys = True , separators = ( "," , ":" ) ) return len ( encoding . encode_ordinary ( wire ) ) tools = json . loads ( Path ( "tool-list.json" ) . read_text ( ) ) [ "result" ] [ "tools" ] actors = [ tool for tool in tools if tool [ "name" ] . startswith ( "automatic--" ) ] print ( "Actor definitions:" , count ( actors ) , "All definitions:" , count ( tools ) ) for tool in actors : print ( tool [ "name" ] , count ( tool ) ) result = json . loads ( Path ( "dataset-call.json" ) . read_text ( ) ) [ "result" ] print ( "Dataset rows:" , len ( result [ "structuredContent" ] [ "items" ] ) ) print ( "MCP result tokens:" , count ( result ) ) Apify run IDs Actor Run ID Dataset ID Companies House qMSAU7AHq8TBKv3QV D5J9OQ69VVQ9LAuk9 Crypto Fear & Greed JflT8tJhN2Q27uRB9 I4iUWE2Og5DJEQHfP Crypto Funding Rates jdBx5FQjy2QYqYtqb 9VlUYZo17bxPcfN70 Wikipedia Pageview Spikes uay8F3LXeRbIdAYmD D24mOqRsFdiYVpZgI YouTube Search mJGdglij0uj3vQr0N ld4lCDerhQxhT3Z9T Google Maps Places b6tgsrLFToi5jMvGB sX7lng7ZWrvzrV70K Google News koGRDmJ8v34DOb8zu UbXzexhWkTd5oXe7v Trustpilot Reviews CUm7Cgt5c38UoGLso ZM9y1SWTCgLIHjrHu Treasury Yield Curve iTfAQZHtF5aCTa2Bb OYhE65XbI2uFZgMkl Inmuebles24 Mexico 1CzUe5PdPjy1dGdZM xKIJfQc3hMhxamIv3 Affiliate disclosure: The Apify Store link carries our referral code. title: How I Cut AI Coding Token Usage by 90% Using Local AST Pruning
author: Toprak
summary: I'm Toprak, a 15-year-old software engineer from Turkey building open-source developer tooling at Siber Akademi. Like many developers using AI coding assistants like Cursor, Claude Desktop, and Windsurf, I constantly hit a major wall on large codebases: Context Window Bloat. The Core Problem: Implementation vs. Interface When you @ tag directories in Cursor Composer, 85-90% of the ingested tokens are function execution bodies (loops, SQL queries, helper transforms) that the AI doesn't need to read just to understand your architecture. The Solution: AST Skeletonization (T-Zero) I spent the last several months engineering T-Zero (v11.11), an open-source local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that prunes multi-language code down to typed AST interface skeletons. 📊 Real Benchmark on 481-File Repository: Raw Codebase Context: 10,998,573 tokens ($32.99 per single Claude 3.5 prompt fill) T-Zero 4-Tier AST Skeletons: 1,319,828 tokens (-88.0% reduction) Focus File Skeleton: -94.6% reduction Local Latency: <400ms (pure local CPU, 0 cloud telemetry) Security: In-memory Shannon entropy scanner (H >= 4.75) detects and redacts hardcoded API keys locally. ⚡ 30-Second Setup in Cursor or Claude Desktop: Add this to your Cursor MCP settings (~/.cursor/mcp.json): { "mcpServers": { "tzero": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "tzero-mcp@latest"] } } } (Or install via pip: pip install tzero-mcp) Everything is 100% free and open-source under the MIT License! I'm currently on a mission to hit my first 100 GitHub Stars ⭐ — if this saves your AI context budget, dropping a star would mean the world to an independent 15-year-old engineer: 👉 GitHub Repo (MIT): https://github.com/toprakahmetaydogmus/TZeroAlgorithm 👉 Interactive Web Playground: https://tzero-indol.vercel.app

title: Turn Newsletter Replies Into a Feedback Log With 40 Lines of Python
author: AI Automation Enterenpeur
summary: Ending a newsletter with one question ("What should we build next?") is one of the cheapest ways to get customer feedback. The hard part isn't getting replies. It's not losing them. Here's a small Python script that checks an inbox for new replies to your newsletter, tags each one by keyword, and appends it to a CSV you can open in any spreadsheet. What it does Connects to your inbox over IMAP. Finds unread messages whose subject matches your newsletter's reply subject. Pulls the plain-text body. Tags it as pricing, bug, feature_request, praise or other. Appends date, sender, tag and the first line to newsletter_replies.csv. No third-party packages. Just the standard library. The code import csv import email import imaplib import os from email . utils import parseaddr SUBJECT = "Re: The Weekly Build" # your newsletter's subject TAGS = { "pricing" : [ "price" , "pricing" , "cost" , "plan" ] , "feature_request" : [ "wish" , "would love" , "feature" , "could you add" ] , "bug" : [ "bug" , "broken" , "error" , "doesn't work" ] , "praise" : [ "love" , "great" , "thanks" , "helpful" ] , } def tag_reply ( text ) : text = text . lower ( ) found = [ tag for tag , words in TAGS . items ( ) if any ( w in text for w in words ) ] return ", " . join ( found ) or "other" def get_body ( msg ) : parts = msg . walk ( ) if msg . is_multipart ( ) else [ msg ] for part in parts : if part . get_content_type ( ) == "text/plain" : payload = part . get_payload ( decode = True ) or b "" return payload . decode ( errors = "ignore" ) return "" def main ( ) : box = imaplib . IMAP4_SSL ( os . environ [ "IMAP_HOST" ] ) box . login ( os . environ [ "IMAP_USER" ] , os . environ [ "IMAP_PASS" ] ) box . select ( "INBOX" ) _ , ids = box . search ( None , f '(UNSEEN SUBJECT "{SUBJECT}")' ) with open ( "newsletter_replies.csv" , "a" , newline = "" ) as f : writer = csv . writer ( f ) for num in ids [ 0 ] . split ( ) : _ , data = box . fetch ( num , "(RFC822)" ) msg = email . message_from_bytes ( data [ 0 ] [ 1 ] ) _ , sender = parseaddr ( msg [ "From" ] ) body = get_body ( msg ) . strip ( ) first_line = body . splitlines ( ) [ 0 ] [ : 200 ] if body else "" writer . writerow ( [ msg [ "Date" ] , sender , tag_reply ( body ) , first_line ] ) box . logout ( ) if __name__ == "__main__" : main ( ) How to run it Set IMAP_HOST, IMAP_USER and IMAP_PASS as environment variables (for Gmail, use imap.gmail.com and an app password), then run: python3 log_replies.py Fetching a message marks it as read, so each reply is logged only once. Schedule it with cron to run every morning: 0 8 * * * cd /path/to/script && python3 log_replies.py Ideas to extend it Strip quoted text (lines starting with ">") so you only keep the new reply. Swap the keyword tagger for an LLM call that returns a tag and a one-sentence summary. Write rows to Google Sheets or your CRM instead of a CSV. Post a Slack or Discord message when a reply is tagged bug. Why bother Keyword tagging won't be perfect, but it turns a pile of unread replies into a sortable list. Once a month, filter by feature_request and you have a ranked, real-words wishlist from your own customers. I build automations like this for businesses and SaaS teams: https://ai-automation-entrepreneur.vercel.app/

title: Markdown to HTML: 0 LLM Tokens for 4 Posts, 23 FAQs Extracted
author: Sungwoo Lee
summary: We needed to publish four manuscripts (43,699 bytes in total) that another project had handed over, and the obvious move was to ask an LLM to turn the markdown into HTML. We wrote a deterministic converter instead. It used zero LLM tokens, extracted 23 FAQ questions automatically, and all four posts passed its built-in checks. The reason is not cost. The manuscripts already contained values that had been cross-checked by hand, such as notice numbers and page numbers, so changing a single character during formatting would itself be a defect. This post covers the rule we use to decide between a script and an LLM, what the converter actually does, and the two publishing traps it closed without anyone having to remember them. Three questions that decide script versus LLM Ask these about the step you are about to automate. A single "yes" means use a script. Question If yes If no Must the same input always give the same output? Script LLM is fine Must source values stay byte-for-byte unchanged? Script LLM is fine Can pass or fail be decided automatically from an exit code? Script LLM is fine Our conversion answered yes to all three. The manuscripts already followed a fixed layout (title, three-line summary, tables, a Q/A list), the rules for turning that layout into tags were unambiguous, and compliance could be checked with plain string searches. Work that needs judgment, such as summarizing, restructuring, or adjusting tone, belongs to the LLM. Moving a fixed format into fixed tags does not. The short version: if judgment is needed, use an LLM; if there is a rule, use a script. There is a cost argument too, but it is the weakest of the three. A few posts are cheap either way, yet an LLM step also gives you a different output on each run and a chance to quietly touch a number. Those two problems are what actually hurt. What the converter does The script takes one markdown file and produces body HTML plus a metadata JSON. If it finds a spec violation it exits with code 1. python -X utf8 scripts/publish/md2bsp.py post.md out/body.html --meta out/meta.json Standard output is two lines. The first is the metadata, the second is the self-check result: {"title": "", "excerpt": "", "faq_count": , "html_len": , "src": "post.md"} self-check: PASS (The full manuscript and converter output checklists are in the original post .) Two numbers catch most formatting accidents. If faq_count differs from what you expect, the Q/A format in the manuscript drifted. If html_len is far smaller than the source, part of the body was not parsed. The converter also removes the H1 from the body and uses the first summary item as the excerpt. Our platform renders the title separately, so leaving the H1 in the body would show it twice. FAQ extraction: the manuscript spec is the parser spec FAQ entries are pulled only from the FAQ section of the body. That keeps the structured data from containing questions the page never shows, which search engines flag as a mismatch. A runnable version of the idea looks like this: import re def extract_faq ( md ) : m = re . search ( r " ##\s*FAQ\s* (.*?)(?= ##\s|\Z)" , md , re . S ) if not m : return [ ] return re . findall ( r "\*\*Q\.\s*(.+?)\*\*\s* \s*A\.\s*(.+?)(?= \s* |\Z)" , m . group ( 1 ) , re . S , ) sample = " ## FAQ **Q. Why a script?** A. Same input, same output. **Q. Cost?** A. Zero tokens. " print ( len ( extract_faq ( sample ) ) ) # 2 The regular expression enforces the format. If the section heading differs, the question line is styled differently, or an answer does not begin with A. , that pair is simply not captured. In other words, the manuscript format becomes the parser's input specification. On these four posts the approach extracted 23 questions with no manual step. Self-checks as exit codes The last block of the converter counts the things that must not ship: a leftover style block, a leftover h1 tag, a leftover TODO marker, a leftover emoji, or a missing title. Any hit makes the process exit with 1. import re def check ( html , title ) : bad = [ ] if "])" , f '<{tag} style="{css}"' , html ) html = html . replace ( f "<{tag}>" , f '<{tag} style="{css}">' ) Tables are wrapped in an overflow-x:auto container in the same pass, so a wide table scrolls instead of pushing the whole page sideways on mobile. The second trap was duplicated JSON-LD, and it came from the handoff document, not from the script. The spec said to put a BlogPosting block in the body. The front end already generates BlogPosting in the head, so following the spec literally would have produced duplicate structured data. Reading the receiving code while building the converter showed that only a FAQPage block belonged in the body. The lesson is about order, not about this spec: read the receiving code before executing a handoff document. A spec is true as of the day it was written, and the system on the other side may have changed since. When this breaks A deterministic converter is only deterministic if the input follows the spec. Otherwise it silently drops things. Failure condition Symptom Fix FAQ heading differs faq_count is 0 Rename the H2 in the manuscript Q/A pairs with no blank line between them Several pairs merge into one Add a blank line between pairs No H1 Exit code 1, "no H1 title" Put a # Title on the first line Manuscripts arrive in different formats each time The rules do not hold Agree on a format first, or keep a human on this step Some limits are worth stating plainly. This converter is built for our blog platform. The per-tag inline styles and the "no style block" rule exist because our renderer hoists styles globally, and another platform may not have that constraint. Markdown parsing relies on an external library and its extensions (tables, sane_lists, nl2br), so a version change can alter the output. And the approach only fits steps that need no judgment: writing the manuscript is still the LLM's job. Split a publishing pipeline along that line, with evidence gathering, machine verification, and layout in scripts and first drafts from the LLM. The original write-up, including the pre-publish checklist for manuscripts and converter output, is here: the full post on my-blog.org . Free tools I keep on my own site: 34 calculators and how-to guides - loans, severance pay, take-home salary, savings vs deposits. New ones go out in one email, no ads.

title: How to Fetch Live Polymarket & Kalshi Prediction Market Odds in Python (Zero API Keys)
author: Khan
summary: Tracking prediction markets across Polymarket and Kalshi usually means maintaining two different APIs, normalizing probability formats ( 0–1 vs cents/bid-ask strings), and manually matching identical questions across venues to spot price spreads. Here is a clean, proxy-free way to pull normalized live odds, 24h volume, liquidity, and cross-venue spread hints from both exchanges in a single Python call. 1. Install the Client pip install apify-client export APIFY_TOKEN = "your_apify_token" 2. Fetch Normalized Polymarket & Kalshi Markets This calls the Polymarket & Kalshi Prediction Markets Unified Scraper directly over HTTP APIs (no headless browser or proxies needed): import os from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ "APIFY_TOKEN" ] ) run = client . actor ( "api-market/prediction-markets-unified" ) . call ( run_input = { "platforms" : [ "polymarket" , "kalshi" ] , "minVolume24h" : 1000 , "maxMarketsPerPlatform" : 50 , "includeCrossMarketMatches" : True , } ) items = list ( client . dataset ( run [ "defaultDatasetId" ] ) . iterate_items ( ) ) print ( f "Fetched {len(items)} normalized markets" ) for m in items [ : 5 ] : print ( m [ "platform" ] , "|" , m [ "question" ] , "| YES:" , m [ "impliedProbPct" ] , "%" ) 3. Or Call It Synchronously via REST / cURL If you don't want an SDK dependency (or want to plug it into n8n, Make, or an AI agent): curl -sS -X POST \ "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/api-market~prediction-markets-unified/run-sync-get-dataset-items" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${APIFY_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"platforms":["polymarket","kalshi"],"maxMarketsPerPlatform":20,"includeCrossMarketMatches":true}' Each returned item follows one flat schema ( platform , question , yesPrice , noPrice , impliedProbPct , spreadBps , volume24h , liquidity , closeTime , and crossMarketMatch when a similar market exists on the other venue). More Proxy-Free Data APIs & Examples I've been building a collection of lightweight, API-first scrapers with Pay-Per-Event pricing and ready-to-run Python/Node/cURL examples in github.com/wOkk93/apify-data-actors : SEC EDGAR Filings & Form D Startup Raises Tracker Greenhouse, Lever & Ashby Unified Jobs Scraper Website Contacts, Emails, Socials & Tech Stack Enricher Podcast Host Emails, RSS & Sponsor Lead Enricher Y Combinator Startups, Batches & Hiring Directory Shopify Store Catalog & B2B Lead Enricher Shopify App Store Reviews & SaaS Defect Intelligence Apple App Store Reviews & Defect Intelligence Google Play Reviews & Defect Intelligence Full catalog: apify.com/api-market — feedback and schema suggestions welcome!

title: Smartlook Alternative for WordPress: Self-Hosted Session Recordings and Heatmaps
author: Hamdi Bk
summary: We build Opti-Behavior, a WordPress plugin; this guide was first published on our blog. The export steps and the checklist are useful whatever tool you pick. Smartlook stopped selling new subscriptions on 31 May 2026 and the platform will be switched off on 30 September 2027, with all remaining data deleted. If your recordings and heatmaps run on Smartlook, you need a Smartlook alternative before your paid plan ends, and you need to export what you want to keep first. This guide gives the official dates, the export route Smartlook documents, a checklist to compare replacements, and the steps to move a WordPress site to a self-hosted tool. The short version: copy your data with the Smartlook APIs before your paid subscription expires, list what you really use (recordings, heatmaps, funnels, events), then test one or two replacements on a real page for a week before your plan runs out. When Smartlook stops: the dates Smartlook has joined Cisco and will wind down as a standalone product. Its features move to Digital Experience Analytics inside Splunk Observability Cloud. The official timeline, published on the Smartlook pricing page (read on 11 November 2026), is: 31 May 2026, End of Sale: no new Smartlook subscriptions are sold. 31 August 2026, End of Contract Renewals: no renewals or expansions for existing accounts. 31 August 2027, Last Day of Support: all remaining paid subscriptions end. 30 September 2027, Platform Decommissioned: the platform is switched off and all remaining customer data is deleted. Between the end of your paid plan and 30 September 2027, Smartlook says you can still use its Free plan, with that plan's limits. Smartlook also states that Splunk will not migrate historical data from Smartlook to Digital Experience Analytics, and that your current subscription will not be transitioned automatically. In practice, the date that matters for you is not 2027. It is the day your own paid plan ends: after it, you lose the paid features and work inside free-plan limits. Write that date down now and plan the switch a few weeks before it. Export your Smartlook data before the shutdown Smartlook's official advice, on the same pricing page FAQ, is to export the data you wish to retain before your paid subscription expires, and in any case no later than 31 August 2027. It says you can create a copy of your data using the Smartlook APIs, and it points to four export resources: Smartlook Reports and Exports (help centre) How to create a REST API token REST API Overview List of available REST API calls For anything these pages do not cover, Smartlook asks customers to contact their Account Manager or support@smartlook.com . Before you start, decide what is worth keeping. Most teams do not need every old recording. They need: The list of events and funnels you defined, so you can rebuild them in the new tool. Reports you shared with clients or your team, as files. The few recordings that explain a known bug or a decision, saved with a note on why they matter. Old behavior data ages fast. A redesign, a new theme or a new checkout makes last year's heatmaps less useful. Your event and funnel definitions keep their value, so export those first. Checklist to choose a Smartlook alternative Feature lists look alike, so compare replacements on the points that change your daily work and your costs. Ask each vendor these five questions and write the answers in one table. 1. Where is the data stored? A hosted service keeps recordings on the vendor's servers. A self-hosted plugin keeps them in your own WordPress database and files. This decides who you list as a processor in your privacy policy, how long data is kept, and what happens to it if the vendor changes its offer, as Smartlook customers are seeing now. 2. What does the free quota really cover? Check what is counted (sessions, page views, recordings), whether bots count, and what happens at the limit: does recording pause, does old data disappear, do features lock? A quota that sounds large can be used up by bot traffic on a small site. 3. How long is the trial, and does it need a card? Two weeks rarely covers a full buying cycle. A longer trial lets you see weekend traffic, a campaign and a few real sales before you decide. 4. Does it understand WooCommerce? If you sell with WooCommerce, check that the tool sees the steps product, cart, checkout and order without custom code, and that it can show where buyers leave. 5. What does it cost in page speed? Do not trust a vendor's speed claim, ours included. Measure it: run PageSpeed Insights on the same page three times with the tool on, then three times with it off, and compare the median. Hotjar, Microsoft Clarity, Mouseflow and Opti-Behavior side by side The table only lists facts published by each vendor on its own page. Plans and limits change, so open the source before you decide. TOOL FREE OPTION (VENDOR'S WORDS) WHERE THE DATA LIVES Hotjar See the vendor's pricing page Vendor-hosted service Microsoft Clarity Free, no traffic limits Vendor-hosted service (Microsoft) Mouseflow Free plan, no credit card required Vendor-hosted service Opti-Behavior Free plugin; 6 months of every Pro feature, no credit card, then 1,000 Pro sessions a month Your own WordPress server If your site is not on WordPress, a hosted tool is the simpler choice: Opti-Behavior is a WordPress plugin and only runs there. If you are on WordPress and want the recordings in your own database, read on. Switch to Opti-Behavior on WordPress in 5 steps Keep Smartlook running in parallel until your export is done and the new tool shows data. Install the Free plugin. In WordPress, go to Plugins → Add New, search "Opti-Behavior", or download it from wordpress.org. Activate it. No snippet to paste in your theme and no external account for the Free plugin. Let tracking run. Visits, pages, sources, click heatmaps and funnels start with the next visitors. If nothing shows after a few visits, a page cache is often serving an old page: purge it once. Start the Pro trial from the plugin. Click "Try Pro Free" in the plugin: 6 months of every Pro feature, no credit card. Then free up to 1,000 sessions a month (bots and spam included), with the data on your own server. At the quota, new Pro recordings pause; nothing is deleted. Read Smart Insights after the first visits. Open Smart Insights once a few dozen sessions are in. It lists what to look at first, so you do not have to watch recordings at random. Then rebuild the funnels you exported from Smartlook. On a WooCommerce shop, the plugin suggests a purchase funnel (shop, product, cart, checkout, order received) that you create in one click. From modules to a report that says what to fix Collecting behavior data is the easy part. The hard part is finding the one problem worth fixing this week. Opti-Behavior connects its modules so that the answer comes to you instead of the other way round. Heatmaps show where visitors click (Free) and how far they scroll (Pro). Session recordings (Pro) show the visit behind a number. Funnels show the step where visitors leave (Free, with more in Pro). Form analytics (Pro) show the field where people give up. Shop counts product → cart → checkout → order on WooCommerce (Free); Pro adds the estimated amount lost per step and payment errors. Error tracking (Pro) logs JavaScript errors with the page and the date. Smart Insights reads these modules together and turns them into findings: a funnel step that loses most visitors, a button nobody clicks, a form field that blocks. The core findings are Free; Smart Insights Pro adds the evidence from recordings, forms, errors, journeys, funnels, Shop and A/B tests. The last step is a report you can act on. The short site report (Free) gives the traffic summary and the 3 most costly issues, each with what to do: On a single page, Page X-Ray (Pro) goes further: it lists what to fix, most costly first, why it matters and what to do for each problem. You can print it or save it as a PDF to share with a client or a developer. A simple routine works: once a week, open the report, fix the first issue, and check the same report seven days later to see whether the number moved. FAQ When does Smartlook close? New sales ended on 31 May 2026, renewals on 31 August 2026, paid subscriptions end by 31 August 2027, and the platform is decommissioned on 30 September 2027, when remaining data is deleted. Source: smartlook.com/pricing. Can I export my Smartlook data? Smartlook says you can copy your data with its APIs and recommends doing it before your paid subscription ends, and no later than 31 August 2027. See its Reports and Exports help page. Is there a free Smartlook alternative on WordPress? Yes. The Opti-Behavior Free plugin gives traffic analytics, click heatmaps, funnels, WooCommerce counters and Smart Insights core with no time limit. Recordings and the other Pro modules come with the Pro trial: 6 months of every Pro feature, no credit card. Where is the data stored? title: I Needed a Square Profile Photo — I Compared 3 Free Image Croppers
author: Zippic
summary: I was updating my profile photo everywhere — GitHub, LinkedIn, a forum I post on — and every single one of them wanted a square image. The photo I liked was a landscape shot from a trip, with me off to one side and a lot of empty sky on the other. I didn't want to install anything for a five-minute job. I just wanted to crop it square, keep my face in the frame, and download a clean result. So I tried three free options and compared them on that one photo. 1. My phone's built-in photo editor I tried my phone's Photos app first, since it was already there. It let me crop to a square, and I could drag the frame around until my face was centred. It worked, but the result stayed on my phone, and I still had to send it to my laptop to use it anywhere else. The square presets were also limited — it was either a free crop or a fixed square, with no way to type in an exact size. For a quick social avatar it was fine, but it felt like a workaround rather than a tool for the job. 2. An online image cropper Next I tried a popular online cropper I found through search. It opened in the browser, I picked my photo, and I could drag a square crop box over it and download the result. The catch was the upload: my photo went to their server before I could crop it. It was just a holiday photo, so it didn't matter much, but I noticed the page was also full of pop-ups and a timer counting down before the download link appeared. It got the job done, but the whole thing felt slower than it needed to be. 3. zippic Then I tried https://zippic.app/image-cropper for the same photo. It runs in your browser. Nothing is uploaded — the file stays on your own device. You open the page, drop the photo in, drag the crop box to a square, and download the result. You can pick a preset ratio like 1:1 or set your own width and height, and it keeps the original quality. I centred the square on my face, downloaded the PNG, and checked it at full size. It was sharp, the colours were unchanged, and the file was ready to upload everywhere. No account, no pop-ups, no waiting. What I compared Square crop? Upload? Signup? Phone photo editor Yes, basic No No Online cropper Yes Yes, to their server No for basic use zippic Yes, preset or custom size No, local No What I ended up doing I kept the original landscape photo untouched. I cropped a square copy with https://zippic.app/image-cropper , checked it at full size, and used it as my profile photo on all three sites. It took about two minutes. The phone editor is fine if you're already on your phone and just need something quick. If I need a square crop at an exact size — or I don't want to upload the photo anywhere — I open zippic now.

title: How to Trim Audio for a Cedar Shore Video — Free, in Your Browser
author: zjch022
summary: A Cedar Shore video — waves on the sand, a sunset walk, kids playing at the water's edge — sounds best when the audio matches the mood. Raw recordings rarely do: they start with wind, end with chatter, and the music runs long. Here is how to trim it to fit, free, in your browser. Step 1: Open AudioCutter Open AudioCutter in your browser. It is a free online audio cutter, and it works on your computer, tablet, or phone. Step 2: Add your audio file Click to open your file — an MP3, WAV, M4A, or another common format. Your file is processed locally in your browser, so it is never uploaded to a server. Step 3: Cut the wind and the chatter Drag the handles on the waveform to select the good middle part of the recording. Trim the windy lead-in at the start and the stray chatter at the end, then listen once to check the cut points. Step 4: Add a short fade A half-second fade-in at the start and a fade-out at the end make the clip sound finished instead of chopped. On beach audio, a gentle fade also smooths the gap between wave sounds. Step 5: Export and sync with your video Export as MP3 or WAV, then drop the clip into your video editor and line it up with the footage. If the music is still longer than the video, trim a verse or the outro rather than speeding the track up — the pace stays natural that way. A few tips that help: Keep the wave sounds low under the music instead of cutting them out completely — they are part of the place. Keep the best 30 to 60 seconds; a short, clean clip beats a long, rambling one. Save the original recording — you can always re-trim it later for a shorter version. That is all there is to it. Open AudioCutter , trim the audio to fit your Cedar Shore video, and the footage finally sounds as calm as the shore itself. Disclosure: I am the developer of AudioCutter, a free online audio cutter at https://audiocutter.me/ that trims MP3, WAV and more right in your browser — no install, no upload, no account needed.

title: How to pull every open job at a company from Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby and Workable (no scraping)
author: Kleb Data
summary: Most startups and a large share of tech companies host their careers page on one of a few applicant tracking systems (ATS): Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable or SmartRecruiters. Each of them publishes a public JSON job-board API meant for embedding. That means you do not need a headless browser or a proxy to get a company's open jobs. You need the right URL. The endpoints ATS Careers page looks like Public JSON Greenhouse boards.greenhouse.io/stripe https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/stripe/jobs?content=true Lever jobs.lever.co/spotify https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/spotify?mode=json Ashby jobs.ashbyhq.com/openai https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/openai?includeCompensation=true Workable apply.workable.com/acme https://apply.workable.com/api/v1/widget/accounts/acme?details=true SmartRecruiters jobs.smartrecruiters.com/acme https://api.smartrecruiters.com/v1/companies/acme/postings?limit=100 Try one: curl -s "https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/stripe/jobs" | jq '.jobs | length' The annoying part Every system names things differently: Greenhouse returns HTML that is escaped twice, and has no employment type. Lever gives createdAt as a millisecond timestamp and puts location under categories . Ashby has a real isRemote flag and a compensation summary; the others mostly do not. SmartRecruiters pages by 100 and its list has no description. If you track 50 companies you end up writing five parsers and a "which ATS is this company on" detector. One schema for all five I wrapped this in a small Apify actor that takes careers URLs (or greenhouse:stripe , or just stripe ) and returns one flat schema: { "company" : "Stripe" , "ats" : "greenhouse" , "title" : "Backend Engineer, Payments" , "location" : "Seattle, San Francisco, New York City" , "remote" : false , "department" : "Engineering" , "postedAt" : "2026-09-09T14:50:29.000Z" , "url" : "https://stripe.com/jobs/search?gh_jid=7123456" } It has filters for title keywords, location, remote-only and "posted after", so a daily run can return only new jobs. A run over six AI companies returned 472 engineering and research jobs in 3 seconds. Actor: https://apify.com/kleb-data/company-jobs-api Ready-made example (OpenAI, Anthropic, Scale AI, Perplexity, Cohere, Databricks): https://apify.com/kleb-data/company-jobs-api/examples/ai-company-jobs-openai-anthropic-more-remote-filter It is free right now apart from Apify platform usage, which is well under a cent per run. What it does not cover Workday, iCIMS and custom career sites. Workday has no public job-board API and blocks server requests, so I left it out rather than work around it. Ideas for using it A daily "new jobs at my target companies" digest Hiring signals for sales: who just opened five data-engineering roles A niche job board for one sector A tool an AI agent can call to answer "what is this company hiring for" If your target companies use an ATS I have not covered and it has a public API, tell me which one.

title: Why Image Compressors Strip Metadata — and How to Prevent It
author: GeoImageTagger
summary: If you have ever run images through a compression pipeline and discovered the EXIF data came out empty, the explanation is usually straightforward: the compressor never handled the metadata in the first place. Image compression operates on pixel data. Metadata — EXIF, IPTC, XMP, GPS coordinates — is stored in structurally separate sections of the file. Whether those sections survive compression is entirely a function of how the tool is built. How Metadata Is Stored (By Format) JPEG JPEG files use marker segments to organize data. The pixel stream starts at the SOS (Start of Scan) marker. Metadata lives in application markers: APP1 ( 0xFFE1 ) — EXIF and XMP payloads APP13 ( 0xFFED ) — IPTC-IIM data APP2 ( 0xFFE2 ) — ICC color profiles Low-level libraries like libjpeg and libjpeg-turbo process only the pixel buffer. They do not automatically parse or carry over APPn markers. To preserve metadata, the developer must explicitly intercept markers during reading (via jpeg_save_markers() ) and reinject them during writing (via jpeg_write_marker() ). Metadata behavior varies by library and configuration. Some image libraries strip metadata by default, while others can preserve it when explicitly configured. For example, Sharp removes metadata by default unless preservation options such as keepMetadata() , keepExif() , or keepXmp() are used. PNG PNG files store metadata in ancillary chunks: tEXt / zTXt / iTXt — text-based metadata (XMP often lives in iTXt ) eXIf — binary EXIF data (added to the PNG specification to match JPEG's EXIF capability) PNG compression itself is lossless — optimizers like OxiPNG reorganize the pixel data more efficiently without changing it. But whether the metadata chunks are preserved depends on the optimizer's implementation. WebP WebP uses a RIFF container with dedicated chunks: EXIF — raw EXIF payload XMP — XML-serialized XMP data (note the trailing space in the FourCC) IPTC is not part of the WebP specification. When converting from JPEG to WebP, EXIF and XMP can be carried over, but IPTC fields have no standard container in WebP. Why Some Compressors Strip Metadata Three common reasons: The compression library does not handle it — if the tool wraps libjpeg without marker handling or uses HTMLCanvasElement.toBlob() without separately preserving and reattaching source metadata, the output file will have no metadata regardless of the input. Deliberate size optimization — some tools strip metadata to save a few kilobytes per file. Format conversion side effects — converting between formats (JPEG → WebP, TIFF → JPEG) can drop metadata fields that the target format does not support. Browser-Side Compression and Metadata Canvas-based workflows operate on decoded pixel data rather than the original file container. Exporting with canvas.toBlob() or canvas.toDataURL() creates a newly encoded image and does not automatically carry over the source file's EXIF, IPTC, or XMP metadata. Applications that need metadata preservation must handle and reattach that metadata separately. Tools that use WebAssembly-based encoders (MozJPEG, libwebp, OxiPNG) can produce better compression results and can handle metadata if the implementation explicitly copies the relevant sections. The GeoImageTagger Image Compressor uses WASM encoders for compression and is designed to preserve supported metadata as a separate step, including post-compression verification. A Verification Workflow If metadata preservation matters for your pipeline, add a verification step: Before compression — inspect the original file's metadata. The Metadata Viewer shows EXIF, IPTC, XMP, and GPS fields for any supported image. After compression — re-inspect the output file. Compare key fields: GPS coordinates, copyright, creator, camera data. If fields are missing — use a metadata editor to restore them, or switch to a compressor that preserves metadata. The Metadata Editor handles writing EXIF, IPTC, and XMP fields. For programmatic workflows, exiftool can copy metadata between files: exiftool -TagsFromFile original.jpg compressed.jpg Preserve vs. Remove: Know Your Use Case Metadata preservation is not always the right choice. Personal photos shared publicly may contain GPS coordinates and device information. For privacy-sensitive images, deliberately removing metadata is the correct approach. The EXIF Remover handles selective removal without re-encoding pixels. Key Takeaways Image compression operates on pixels; metadata survival depends on the tool JPEG metadata lives in APP1 / APP13 markers — easily preserved if the tool handles them PNG metadata lives in ancillary chunks — lossless compression should not affect them, but verify WebP supports EXIF and XMP but not IPTC Canvas-based export does not automatically preserve source EXIF/IPTC/XMP metadata WASM-based compressors can preserve metadata if designed to Always verify metadata after compression for critical workflows For the full guide, see How to Compress Images Without Losing EXIF, GPS, IPTC or XMP Metadata .

title: I re-ran a rival's memory benchmark. It tied mine. Here is the interesting part.
author: Calas Automations
summary: I build Monomem, shared memory for AI coding agents. It records which app wrote each note and holds suspicious writes until a person looks. On LongMemEval-S, a standard long-term-memory test, a well-known memory project (agentmemory) publishes 84.7%. I re-ran its own evaluation on the same data file and got 84.7% back, exactly. Monomem scored 86.0% (404 of 470 questions). Question by question, 14 were answered only by Monomem and 8 only by agentmemory. That gap is not significant (exact McNemar test, p = 0.29). It is a tie. Two more things I will not hide: Monomem's ranking was tuned on half of this question set, so the fairer figure is the other half: R@5 97.5, Rall@5 86.2. The repo says so. Another system, Vestige, reports a higher score than mine (its own number, which I have not re-run). It is named in the docs. Why post a tie? Because memory search is turning into a commodity. What I think still matters is trust: who wrote a note, whether an outside web page could have poisoned it, and whether you can undo it. Monomem's own attack check ( monomem check --attacks ) replays 26 known poisoning attacks on a copy of your store. Two are known misses (a reworded override, and self-poisoning), and the README lists them next to the headline number. It is pattern matching, so a reworded attack it does not know can get through. Everything runs on your computer in one file: no cloud, no account. MIT licence. Beta, not independently security-reviewed. Reproduce the numbers: monomem bench --longmemeval ... --per-question out.ndjson (instructions in docs/BENCHMARK.md). If you can beat or break it, tell me. Repo: https://github.com/calasdan-sketch/monomem Using it at work? Team setup and support: https://calasautomations.com/devtools/monomem/#teams

title: Has Anyone Tried Combining NCM with Apple's Neural Engine (ANE)?
author: Giancarlo Vizhnay
summary: Has Anyone Experimented with NCM + ANE? I've been curious about whether Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) , a concept-based generative modeling architecture, could benefit from Apple's Neural Engine (ANE) . With Apple Silicon offering dedicated hardware for machine learning, I'm wondering whether NCM could be optimized for local inference through Core ML. Some Questions Worth Exploring ANE Acceleration: Has anyone successfully deployed an NCM architecture on Apple's Neural Engine? FP16 Precision: Could half-precision inference improve execution speed without significantly affecting prediction accuracy? Core ML Compatibility: What challenges might arise when converting NCM components from PyTorch to Core ML? Hardware Limitations: Could an M4 MacBook Air with 16GB unified memory handle this architecture efficiently? Performance: Would the ANE offer meaningful advantages over CPU or GPU inference for this type of model? Why This Interests Me Much of the machine learning discussion focuses on GPUs and CUDA, but Apple's Neural Engine presents another possibility for local AI research. I'm particularly interested in whether concept-based generative architectures could take advantage of dedicated neural hardware. What Does the Community Think? Has anyone attempted something similar? Are there existing implementations, benchmarks, or research exploring NCM on Apple Silicon? I'd be interested in hearing from anyone experimenting with NCM, Core ML, or Apple Neural Engine acceleration.

title: Abaixo dos 60 mil: o Bitcoin caiu num dia de pânico nas bolsas, e eu não apertei nenhum botão (#20)
author: Leonardo Branco
summary: Abaixo dos 60 mil: o Bitcoin caiu num dia de pânico nas bolsas, e eu não apertei nenhum botão (#20) Em 20 de novembro de 2026, uma sexta-feira, eu olhei o mercado de hora em hora, do fim da manhã até as 20h, no horário de Brasília. Em todas as verificações, a resposta foi a mesma: esperar em dólar. Não fiz nenhuma operação. O que o mercado fez Na Binance, o Bitcoin começou o dia perto de 62 mil, já pesado. De manhã, tentou repicar, mas foi rejeitado em 62.179. Na vela das 12h, perdeu os 60 mil com um volume cerca de 5,7 vezes o normal. Às 13h, marcou 58.769. Às 16h, foi a 57.778, a mínima do dia. No começo da noite, repicou até 59.411, mas com volume baixo. Por volta das 20h40, estava em 59.042, cerca de 4,5% abaixo de 24 horas antes. O Ethereum caiu mais: perto de 7,3% em 24 horas, para 1.624, com mínima de 1.581. A Solana caiu cerca de 5,2%, para 69,33, com mínima de 67,15. No noticiário que acompanhei: saída recorde dos fundos de Bitcoin, medo de alta de juros e uma venda generalizada nas bolsas americanas, com o S&P 500 perto de −3,7%, a Nasdaq perto de −5% e o índice de volatilidade (VIX) acima de 32. As liquidações em cripto passaram de 1 bilhão de dólares. As oportunidades que eu recusei O repique da manhã, a 62.179, foi rejeitado sem volume. Depois da mínima das 16h, a vela deixou um pavio para baixo, que às vezes marca um fundo. Na hora seguinte, não veio continuação. O repique das 18h, até 59.411, fechou com volume baixo. Comprar qualquer um desses momentos seria apostar no fundo sem sinal. Nenhum deles tinha o que a minha regra pede: um ganho esperado de pelo menos duas vezes a perda possível, já contando as taxas, com perda máxima de cerca de 1% do caixa. O retrato do caixa Por volta das 20h40, o caixa tinha 15,90 USDT, mais restos de BNB e Bitcoin: cerca de 16,06 dólares, sem nenhuma ordem aberta. No começo do experimento, eram cerca de 17,05. Sigo uns 5,8% abaixo. O centavo a menos que ontem veio só da queda do valor desses restos. O que eu aprendi Três dias seguidos de queda, e hoje o Bitcoin caiu quase 5%. Se eu tivesse comprado no primeiro repique "barato" da semana, estaria bem mais abaixo. Esperar parece não fazer nada, mas num dia assim é uma decisão. O difícil vai ser reconhecer a hora em que esperar deixa de ser a decisão certa. E você? Num dia de pânico como esse, você procura o fundo para comprar ou espera o mercado mostrar que parou de cair? A história completa deste experimento está virando um e-book: Um caixa de dezessete dólares.
